title: Databases, presentations and file management
objective: Design simple databases, build clear presentations, and manage and share files across applications.
body:
The Computer Applications test also checks that you can store information in a database, present it with slides and move it safely between programs. These items reward precise vocabulary.

**Database structure.** A *database* is an organized collection of related data. A *table* stores data about one subject. Each *record* (row) describes one item, such as one customer, and each *field* (column) holds one attribute, such as a phone number. Every field has a *data type*, such as short text, number, currency, date/time or yes/no. Store ZIP codes and phone numbers as text, because they are never used in math and may begin with a zero. A *primary key* uniquely identifies each record, such as a customer ID. A *foreign key* in another table refers to that key, creating a *relationship*; in a *one-to-many* relationship, one customer can have many orders.

**Database objects.**
- *Query*: asks a question of the data, such as all orders over $100 placed in May, using *criteria* and sorting.
- *Form*: a user-friendly screen for entering and viewing one record at a time.
- *Report*: a formatted printout or summary of data, often grouped with subtotals.

**Presentations.** Plan the message before the slides. Keep text short, using a guideline such as *6x6* (no more than about six bullets of about six words each), choose high-contrast colors and readable fonts, generally 24 points or larger for body text, and present one main idea per slide. The *slide master* controls the layout, fonts and logo on every slide, so a change there updates the whole deck. A *transition* is the effect between slides; an *animation* is an effect applied to an object on a slide. *Speaker notes* hold your talking points without cluttering the screen.

**Files and integration.** A *file extension* identifies the file type: .docx (word processing), .xlsx (spreadsheet), .pptx (presentation), .pdf (fixed layout for sharing) and .csv (plain-text data separated by commas, easy to import into a spreadsheet or database). When you place spreadsheet data in a report, *linking* keeps a connection so the report updates when the source file changes, while *embedding* stores a separate copy that does not update. Use clear file names and folders, and protect work with regular backups, such as the 3-2-1 rule: three copies, on two types of storage, with one kept off-site or in the cloud.

**Common mistake:** confusing a record with a field. A record is a whole row about one item; a field is one category of data that appears in every row.
examples: A school store database has a Products table (primary key ProductID) and a Sales table that stores ProductID as a foreign key. One product can appear in many sales: a one-to-many relationship.
A query with the criteria Grade = 11 and Hours >= 20 lists every junior who has logged at least 20 volunteer hours, and a report then groups them by homeroom with totals.
A treasurer links a budget chart from a spreadsheet into the monthly slide deck. When the spreadsheet is updated, the chart in the presentation updates too.

questions.stem: In a customer table, which field is the best choice for the primary key?
questions.explanation: A primary key must be unique for every record, and an assigned ID guarantees that. Many customers can share a last name, city or purchase date.

questions.stem: Which data type is best for a ZIP code field that includes values such as 02134?
questions.explanation: ZIP codes are never used in calculations, and a number field would drop the leading zero. Text stores the code exactly as entered.

questions.stem: A manager wants to retrieve only the orders over $100 placed in May, sorted by amount. Which database object should be created?
questions.explanation: A query uses criteria to select and sort specific records. A form is for entering or viewing one record at a time, and a report formats data for printing.

questions.stem: One customer can place many orders, and each order belongs to exactly one customer. Which relationship exists between the Customers and Orders tables?
questions.explanation: Each customer record can match many order records, but each order matches only one customer, which is a one-to-many relationship.

questions.stem: A designer wants the company logo in the same position on every slide and wants to update it in only one place if the logo changes. Which tool should be used?
questions.explanation: Items placed on the slide master appear on every slide that uses its layouts, so one change updates the whole presentation.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the difference between a transition and an animation?
choices: A transition is the effect between slides; an animation is an effect on an object within a slide
An animation is the effect between slides; a transition moves an object within a slide
Transitions appear only in printed handouts; animations appear only on screen
Animations can be applied only to the title slide of a presentation
questions.explanation: Transitions control how one slide changes to the next. Animations make individual objects, such as a bullet or chart, enter, exit or move.

questions.stem: Monthly figures in a spreadsheet change often, and a report must always show the latest numbers. How should the data be placed in the report?
questions.explanation: A linked object stays connected to the source file and updates when the spreadsheet changes. An embedded object is a separate copy that does not update.

questions.stem: A team must send a finished brochure that should look the same on any device and be hard to change by accident. Which file format is best?
questions.explanation: PDF files keep a fixed layout across devices and are not easily edited by accident. CSV and TXT files hold plain text and lose all design.

flashcards.definition: One row in a database table containing all the fields of data about a single item, such as one customer.
A field whose value uniquely identifies each record in a database table, such as a student ID.
A database object that retrieves records meeting set criteria, often sorted or combined from several tables.
The top-level slide that controls layouts, fonts, colors and logos for every slide in a presentation.
Data placed in a file that stays connected to its source file and updates when the source changes.
